set.body:
META-BEAD. This does not report a defect; it fixes the criterion by which the other usability beads may be remediated. Filing it before remediation starts because the obvious fixes are the dangerous ones.

The accessibility problem in this package is overwhelmingly a VOCABULARY problem, and the naive fix - 'use simpler words' - would destroy real guarantees. Every unfamiliar term in the docs falls into exactly one of two classes, and they require opposite treatment:

  CLASS I - an existing idea wearing a new name.
    A standard term exists, means the same thing, and the field already knows it.
    Nothing is lost by switching. These are pure cost: they tax every reader and
    buy nothing.
    Suspected members, to be confirmed by the vignette reviewer:
      'declared partitions'          -> runs / sessions / folds
      'declared spatial measurement' -> searchlight / ROI / voxel
      'native features'              -> voxels
      'experimental effects'         -> condition betas / contrast estimates

  CLASS II - a genuine distinction with no standard name.
    The 0.1 engineering programme kept these explicit ON PURPOSE and the unfamiliar
    word is the only thing holding the distinction open. Renaming or collapsing these
    would reintroduce exactly the confusions that work was built to prevent.
    Suspected members:
      the plan / materialize split      (introduction.Rmd:337-339 is explicit that
                                         'storage or workspace policy never changes
                                         the semantic distinction')
      capability gating                 (a default would be a hidden claim about a
                                         capability the user never declared)
      coherent vs configuration energy  (a real decomposition, not a restatement)
      retention of negative estimates   (an inferential commitment, not a display choice)

THE RULE:
  Class I gets renamed to the field's word. Cheap, safe, high leverage.
  Class II gets TAUGHT, never renamed and never defaulted away. The remedy for a
  Class II term is a worked example where the reader watches the distinction matter -
  not a friendlier synonym, and not a convenience wrapper that hides the choice.

Stated negatively, because this is the failure mode I expect: a one-line entry point
that collapses relation -> compile_frame -> plan_geometry -> geometry would score
extremely well on every accessibility metric in the other beads and would silently
convert a Class II distinction into a default. If such a wrapper is built, it must make
the plan/materialize choice VISIBLE rather than absent - a named argument the user sees
and can read about, not an inferred behaviour.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN THE INDIVIDUAL FINDINGS: the current docs fail not because
they are precise but because they present Class I and Class II vocabulary at identical
weight, at first contact, with no signal about which is which. A reader spending effort
on 'native features' has no way to know that term is free to ignore while 'coherent
versus configuration' is the actual content. Fixing the ratio is most of the accessibility
win, and it costs none of the rigour.

FOR claude-review: you have the best map of which guarantees are load-bearing. If you
read only one bead from this workstream, read this one, and correct my Class II list.
Anything you move from Class I to Class II is a rename I will not propose. I would rather
over-classify into Class II and lose some accessibility than flatten a distinction you
spent 48 passes defending.
set.title: Repair criterion: separate load-bearing vocabulary from renamed-standard vocabulary before touching any prose
